about: 1P1 is the Part IA Engineering Tripos course in thermofluid mechanics. On the Department's 2025-26 syllabus page (the 2026-27 page could not be checked; the 2024-25 page has the same content) it runs as 24 lectures, two a week, across Lent term and the first weeks of Easter term. Part I (10 lectures) covers fluid mechanics: hydrostatics, control volumes, the steady momentum equation, Bernoulli's equation and curved streamlines. Part II (14 lectures) covers thermodynamics: the First and Second Laws, perfect gases, entropy, the steady flow energy equation and the Otto, Diesel and Joule cycles. This pack follows that order, grouping some short lecture blocks into single topics.
topics: Introduction to fluids, fluid statics and buoyancy
Control volumes, mass conservation and the steady momentum equation
Bernoulli's equation, flow measurement and open channel flow
Thermodynamic fundamentals, the First Law and perfect gases
The Second Law, heat engines, the Carnot cycle and temperature
Reciprocating engines: the Otto and Diesel cycles
Control volume thermodynamics: the SFEE and the Second Law for flows
Gas turbines and jet engines: the Joule cycle

notes.h: What a fluid is, hydrostatics and buoyancy
notes.body:
A fluid is a substance that deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small. A solid resists shear by deforming a finite amount; a fluid at rest therefore cannot carry any shear stress at all. That single fact drives the whole of hydrostatics: in a fluid at rest the only stress is pressure, which acts normal to every surface and is the same in all directions at a point.

Forces in fluids
- Body forces act on the whole volume (gravity, ρg per unit volume).
- Surface forces act on boundaries: pressure (normal) and viscous shear (tangential, only when the fluid moves).
- Useful vocabulary for later: streamline, lift (force perpendicular to the oncoming flow), drag (force parallel to it), steady flow (nothing changes with time at a fixed point).

The hydrostatic equation
Balancing forces on a small vertical element of fluid gives dp/dz = −ρg, with z measured upwards. For a liquid of constant density this integrates to p = p_atm + ρgh, where h is depth below the free surface.
- Gauge pressure is pressure measured relative to atmospheric; absolute pressure includes p_atm (about 1.013 bar).
- Pressure depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container (the "hydrostatic paradox").
- Example: at 10 m depth in water, gauge pressure = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98.1 kPa, roughly one extra atmosphere.

Manometers and barometers
A U-tube manometer containing a dense liquid (density ρ_m) connecting two points in a fluid of density ρ gives p_A − p_B = (ρ_m − ρ)gh, where h is the difference in manometer levels. Work it methodically: start at one end, add ρgΔz going down and subtract going up, and equate pressures at the same level in a continuous body of the same fluid. Example: mercury (13,600 kg/m³) under water with h = 0.1 m gives Δp = 12,600 × 9.81 × 0.1 ≈ 12.4 kPa. A mercury barometer balances atmospheric pressure against a column with a near vacuum above it, so p_atm = ρgh (about 760 mm of mercury).

Forces on submerged surfaces
The resultant hydrostatic force on a plane surface equals the pressure at its centroid times its area: F = ρg h_c A. It acts at the centre of pressure, which is below the centroid because pressure grows with depth.
- Vertical rectangular gate of width b with water to depth H on one side: F = ½ρgbH², acting at 2H/3 below the surface (the centroid of the triangular pressure distribution).
- Example: H = 3 m, b = 2 m gives F = 0.5 × 1000 × 9.81 × 2 × 9 ≈ 88.3 kN, acting 2 m below the surface.
- For curved surfaces, find horizontal and vertical components separately: the horizontal component equals the force on the vertical projection; the vertical component equals the weight of fluid above the surface (real or imaginary).

Buoyancy (Archimedes' principle)
A body wholly or partly immersed experiences an upward force equal to the weight of fluid displaced, acting through the centroid of the displaced volume (the centre of buoyancy). It arises simply because pressure is greater on the lower surfaces than the upper ones. A floating body displaces its own weight, so the fraction submerged equals ρ_body/ρ_fluid; wood of density 600 kg/m³ floats 60% submerged in fresh water.

Exam tips: always draw the pressure distribution and state whether you are using gauge or absolute pressure; check units (1 bar = 10⁵ Pa) and remember that the centre of pressure is never above the centroid.

notes.h: Control volumes, continuity and the steady momentum equation
notes.body:
Thermofluid problems can be posed in two ways. A system is a fixed quantity of matter that we follow as it moves; its boundary moves with it. A control volume (CV) is a region of space that we choose, with fluid flowing in and out across its control surface. For flowing fluids the CV is almost always more convenient, because we can put the boundary where we know things (inlets, outlets, walls).

Conservation of mass
For a steady flow nothing inside the CV changes with time, so the mass flow in equals the mass flow out.
- Mass flow rate through an area with uniform velocity normal to it: ṁ = ρAV.
- For a single inlet and outlet: ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂. For an incompressible fluid this becomes A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ = Q, the volume flow rate.
- Example: water in a 100 mm pipe at 2 m/s entering a 50 mm pipe: area falls by a factor 4, so velocity rises to 8 m/s.

The steady flow momentum equation
Applying Newton's second law to a CV in steady flow gives: the net force on the fluid in the CV equals the rate at which momentum leaves minus the rate at which it enters.
- Vector form: ΣF = Σ(ṁV)out − Σ(ṁV)in.
- ΣF includes pressure forces on the control surface, forces from walls or vanes (the unknown we usually want), and the weight of the fluid in the CV if relevant.
- Resolve in x and y separately. Velocities are vectors, so sign matters: a jet leaving in the −x direction carries negative x-momentum.

Standard method
- Draw the CV and mark all flows in and out with velocities and pressures.
- Mark the unknown force from the solid on the fluid, with an assumed direction.
- Write mass conservation, then momentum in each direction.
- The force on the solid is equal and opposite (Newton's third law).
- Use gauge pressures: atmospheric pressure acting all round a closed surface gives no net force.

Worked example: jet striking a plate
A water jet of diameter 50 mm and speed 20 m/s hits a large flat plate normally and spreads out radially. A = π × 0.025² = 1.963 × 10⁻³ m², so ṁ = 1000 × 1.963 × 10⁻³ × 20 = 39.3 kg/s. All the jet's x-momentum is destroyed (the outflow is perpendicular), and the jet is at atmospheric pressure, so the force on the plate is F = ṁV = 39.3 × 20 ≈ 785 N.
- If a curved vane turns the jet through 180° with no loss of speed, the momentum change is doubled: F = 2ṁV.

Other classic applications
- Pipe bends and nozzles: include p₁A₁ and p₂A₂ acting inward on the CV at each cut, then solve for the force needed to hold the fitting in place.
- Sudden expansion: momentum plus continuity show that a head loss of (V₁ − V₂)²/2g must occur, which Bernoulli alone cannot predict.
- Rockets and jet engines: thrust arises from the momentum flux of the exhaust.

Exam tips: the most common errors are omitting pressure forces at inlets and outlets, mixing up the force on the fluid with the force on the solid, and forgetting that velocity is a vector. Always state your sign convention.

Bernoulli's equation relates pressure, speed and height along a streamline. Applying Newton's second law to a small element moving along a streamline, in steady, inviscid flow, gives on integration (for constant density):
- p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant along a streamline.
- Dividing by ρg gives "heads": p/ρg + V²/2g + z = H, the total head.
- The stagnation (total) pressure p₀ = p + ½ρV² is the pressure reached if the flow is brought to rest without losses.

When it applies
- Steady flow.
- Incompressible (a good approximation for gases below a Mach number of about 0.3).
- Negligible viscous effects (no friction losses), and no work or heat exchange with the flow (no pumps or turbines between the two points).
- Along a streamline; if the flow upstream is uniform (irrotational), the constant is the same on all streamlines.
It does not apply across mixing regions, sudden expansions, or through machines. In those cases use the momentum equation or energy equation instead.

Flow measurement
- Pitot tube: measures stagnation pressure; with a static tapping, V = √(2(p₀ − p)/ρ). Air (1.2 kg/m³) with p₀ − p = 600 Pa gives V ≈ 31.6 m/s.
- Venturi meter: a contraction raises speed and lowers pressure. Combining continuity with Bernoulli: V₂ = √[2(p₁ − p₂) / (ρ(1 − (A₂/A₁)²))] and Q = A₂V₂.
- Example: water, 100 mm pipe, 50 mm throat, Δp = 15 kPa. (A₂/A₁)² = 0.0625, so V₂ = √(30/0.9375) = √32 ≈ 5.66 m/s and Q ≈ 1.96 × 10⁻³ × 5.66 ≈ 0.0111 m³/s (11.1 L/s). Real meters use a discharge coefficient slightly below 1.
- Discharge from a tank (Torricelli): free surface and jet both at atmospheric pressure, so V = √(2gh); 5 m of head gives about 9.9 m/s. A sharp-edged orifice jet contracts to a vena contracta, so the actual flow is less than area × ideal speed.

Open channel flow
In a channel with a free surface, pressure is hydrostatic across the depth, so the free surface acts as a streamline at atmospheric pressure. Per unit width, continuity gives q = Vh, and Bernoulli along the surface gives h + V²/2g = constant (the specific energy E, for a level bed).
- Froude number Fr = V/√(gh). Fr < 1 is subcritical (deep, slow); Fr > 1 is supercritical (shallow, fast). For a given q, E is minimum at the critical depth, where Fr = 1.
- Sluice gate: the flow accelerates from deep, slow subcritical flow upstream to shallow, fast supercritical flow downstream with (ideally) no energy loss. Solving h₁ + q²/(2gh₁²) = h₂ + q²/(2gh₂²) gives q.
- Example: h₁ = 2 m, h₂ = 0.4 m gives q² = 2g(h₁ − h₂)/(1/h₂² − 1/h₁²) = 19.62 × 1.6/6, so q ≈ 2.29 m²/s.
- The force on the gate cannot come from Bernoulli; use the momentum equation with hydrostatic pressure forces ½ρgh² per unit width.

Exam tips: state the assumptions each time you use Bernoulli, choose points where you know most quantities (free surfaces, jets in air at atmospheric pressure, large reservoirs where V ≈ 0) and combine with continuity.

notes.h: Curved streamlines, the Coanda and Magnus effects, and lift
notes.body:
When fluid moves along a curved path, something must supply the centripetal acceleration V²/R towards the centre of curvature. In a fluid that force comes from a pressure gradient across the streamlines. Applying Newton's second law normal to a streamline (ignoring gravity) gives:
- ∂p/∂n = ρV²/R, where n points away from the centre of curvature.
- So pressure increases as you move outwards, away from the centre of curvature. Equivalently, pressure is lowest on the inside of a bend.
- If streamlines are straight and parallel (R → ∞), there is no pressure gradient across them apart from hydrostatic effects. That is why a free jet emerging into the atmosphere has atmospheric pressure throughout.

Consequences
- Flow round a bend in a pipe or channel: higher pressure at the outer wall. In a river bend this drives secondary flows that pile sediment on the inside.
- A free vortex, or water swirling down a plughole: the pressure falls towards the centre, so the free surface dips.
- Airfoils: streamlines curve over the upper surface, so pressure at the surface is below the free stream pressure, giving suction on top.

The Coanda effect
A jet blown tangentially along a convex curved surface tends to follow the surface rather than continue straight. For the jet to curve, the pressure at the surface must be below the ambient pressure on the jet's outer edge, and that low pressure holds the jet against the surface. The surface is pulled towards the jet. Familiar demonstrations include a stream of tap water clinging to the back of a spoon. Engineering uses include flap blowing on aircraft wings and some ventilation devices. If the curvature is too sharp, the boundary layer cannot cope with the adverse pressure gradient and the jet separates.

The Magnus effect
A spinning cylinder or ball in a stream drags fluid round with it through viscous action. On one side the surface moves with the flow, on the other against it. The flow speeds up on the side moving with the stream and slows on the other, and the separation point is displaced. The result is a net sideways force: a ball with topspin dips, backspin produces lift, and sidespin makes a football or tennis ball swerve. Flettner rotor ships use the same effect for propulsion.

Circulation and lift
- Circulation Γ is the line integral of velocity round a closed loop: Γ = ∮ V·dl. It measures the net "swirl" of the flow round a body.
- A lifting body (spinning cylinder or airfoil) has a non-zero circulation: flow is faster over one side than the other.
- Background (a standard result, not named on the syllabus page): for two-dimensional flow, the Kutta–Joukowski theorem gives lift per unit span L′ = ρVΓ, where V is the free stream speed. The force is perpendicular to the free stream.
- For an airfoil, the sharp trailing edge fixes the circulation: the flow must leave the trailing edge smoothly (the Kutta condition).
- Lift and drag are usually expressed as coefficients: C_L = L/(½ρV²A) and C_D = D/(½ρV²A), with A a reference area.

Exam tips: the key physical argument is "curved streamlines need a pressure gradient". Be ready to explain the Coanda and Magnus effects in words and sketches, and to say which way the pressure rises across a curved flow.

notes.h: Thermodynamic basics, the First Law and perfect gases
notes.body:
Thermodynamics deals with energy, its transfer as heat and work, and the properties of substances. Classical thermodynamics treats matter as a continuum and works with macroscopic properties; the molecular view explains these properties statistically.

Fundamental concepts
- System: a fixed mass (closed system). Its surroundings are everything else.
- Property: a measurable characteristic of the state (p, v, T, u, h, s). Specific properties are per unit mass.
- State: fixed by the values of the properties. For a simple pure substance in equilibrium, any two independent properties fix the state (the two-property rule).
- Equilibrium: no unbalanced driving forces (mechanical, thermal, chemical). Properties are only defined for equilibrium states.
- Heat and work are energy in transit across the boundary. They are not properties: their values depend on the path, not just the end states.

The First Law for a closed system
Energy is conserved. Using the convention that Q is heat supplied to the system and W is work done by the system:
- Q − W = ΔE, where E = U + kinetic + potential energy (usually just U).
- Per unit mass: q − w = Δu.
- For a cycle the system returns to its initial state, so ΔE = 0 and ∮δQ = ∮δW.
- For an adiabatic process Q = 0 and W = −ΔU.
- Reversible work done by a fluid at a moving boundary: W = ∫p dV.

Pure substances and properties
A pure substance has uniform chemical composition and can exist as solid, liquid or vapour. Properties for water and steam are read from tables; for gases at modest pressures the perfect gas model is excellent. Enthalpy is defined as H = U + pV (h = u + pv) and is the natural energy property for constant-pressure and flow processes. Specific heats: c_v = (∂u/∂T)_v and c_p = (∂h/∂T)_p.

Perfect gases
- Equation of state: pv = RT, with R = R̄/M (universal gas constant 8.314 kJ/kmol K divided by molar mass). For air R ≈ 287 J/kg K.
- u and h depend on T only (a semi-perfect gas); if c_p and c_v are also constant, the gas is perfect: Δu = c_vΔT, Δh = c_pΔT.
- c_p − c_v = R and γ = c_p/c_v. For air c_p ≈ 1005 J/kg K, c_v ≈ 718 J/kg K, γ ≈ 1.4.

Processes for a perfect gas (reversible)
- Constant volume (isochoric): w = 0, q = c_vΔT.
- Constant pressure (isobaric): w = pΔv, q = c_pΔT.
- Isothermal: Δu = 0, so q = w = RT ln(v₂/v₁) = RT ln(p₁/p₂).
- Polytropic, pvⁿ = constant: w = (p₁v₁ − p₂v₂)/(n − 1) = R(T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1).
- Reversible adiabatic (isentropic): n = γ, so pv^γ = constant and T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ) = (v₁/v₂)^(γ−1).
- Example: air compressed isentropically from 1 bar, 300 K to 10 bar reaches T₂ = 300 × 10^0.2857 ≈ 579 K. In a closed system the work input is c_v(T₂ − T₁) ≈ 718 × 279 ≈ 200 kJ/kg.

Exam tips: state your sign convention for W, use kelvin throughout, and sketch the process on p–v axes. Check whether the question is a closed system (use u and ∫p dv) or a flow process (use h, see SFEE).

notes.h: The Second Law, heat engines and the Carnot cycle
notes.body:
The First Law says energy is conserved but says nothing about direction. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse; work can be wholly converted to heat by friction, but heat cannot be wholly converted to work in a cycle. The Second Law captures these one-way features.

Reversible and irreversible processes
A reversible process is one that could be reversed leaving no change in the system or surroundings. It is an ideal limit. Sources of irreversibility include:
- friction and viscous dissipation;
- heat transfer across a finite temperature difference;
- unrestrained (free) expansion;
- mixing, combustion and electrical resistance.

Statements of the Second Law
- Kelvin–Planck: it is impossible for a device operating in a cycle to produce net work while exchanging heat with a single reservoir. Every heat engine must reject some heat.
- Clausius: it is impossible for a device operating in a cycle to transfer heat from a colder to a hotter body with no other effect. A refrigerator needs a work input.
- The two statements are equivalent: violating one allows a device that violates the other.

Heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps
- Heat engine: takes Q_H from a hot reservoir, rejects Q_C to a cold one, and produces W = Q_H − Q_C. Thermal efficiency η = W/Q_H = 1 − Q_C/Q_H.
- Refrigerator: uses work W to extract Q_C from the cold space. Coefficient of performance COP_R = Q_C/W.
- Heat pump: the same machine, judged on heat delivered: COP_HP = Q_H/W = COP_R + 1.

The Carnot cycle and Carnot's principle
The Carnot cycle consists of two reversible isothermal processes (heat exchange at T_H and T_C) and two reversible adiabatic processes. Carnot's principle states:
- No engine working between two reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine working between the same reservoirs.
- All reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency.
- For a reversible engine Q_C/Q_H = T_C/T_H, so η_Carnot = 1 − T_C/T_H.
- Reversible COPs: COP_R = T_C/(T_H − T_C), COP_HP = T_H/(T_H − T_C).
- Example: between 800 K and 300 K, η_max = 1 − 300/800 = 0.625. A heat pump lifting heat from 0 °C (273 K) to 20 °C (293 K) has an ideal COP of 293/20 ≈ 14.7; real heat pumps achieve far less because of finite temperature differences in the heat exchangers and other irreversibilities.

Temperature
- Zeroth Law: two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other. This justifies thermometers.
- Empirical scales depend on a thermometric property (mercury expansion, resistance) and different thermometers can disagree between fixed points.
- The perfect gas scale uses a constant-volume gas thermometer in the low-pressure limit: T ∝ p.
- The thermodynamic temperature scale is defined from the Carnot result Q_C/Q_H = T_C/T_H, so it is independent of any substance. It coincides with the perfect gas scale. The triple point of water is 273.16 K; since 2019 the kelvin has been defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant.

Exam tips: always use absolute temperatures in Carnot formulas; when asked if a proposed device is possible, compare its claimed efficiency or COP with the Carnot value, or check the entropy change of the universe.

Entropy turns the Second Law into a quantitative tool.

The Clausius inequality
For any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, where T is the temperature at the boundary where heat δQ crosses. The equality holds for a reversible cycle; the inequality for an irreversible one. It follows from applying Carnot's principle to the many small heat transfers round a cycle.

Definition of entropy
Because ∮δQ_rev/T = 0 for any reversible cycle, the integral of δQ_rev/T between two states is independent of path, so it defines a property:
- dS = δQ_rev/T, with units J/K (specific entropy s in J/kg K).
- For any process: S₂ − S₁ ≥ ∫δQ/T. The difference is the entropy generated by irreversibility: S₂ − S₁ = ∫δQ/T + S_gen, with S_gen ≥ 0.
- A reversible adiabatic process is isentropic (ΔS = 0). An irreversible adiabatic process always increases entropy.

The Tds equations and perfect gases
Combining the First Law (reversible form: δq = du + p dv) with δq_rev = T ds gives relations between properties, valid for any process between equilibrium states:
- T ds = du + p dv
- T ds = dh − v dp
For a perfect gas, substituting du = c_v dT, dh = c_p dT and pv = RT and integrating:
- s₂ − s₁ = c_v ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(v₂/v₁)
- s₂ − s₁ = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁)
Setting Δs = 0 recovers the isentropic relations, e.g. T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ).

Worked examples
- Heating 1 kg of air at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K: Δs = 1005 ln 2 ≈ 697 J/kg K.
- Free (Joule) expansion of air into a vacuum doubling its volume, insulated: Q = 0, W = 0, so ΔU = 0 and T is unchanged. Yet Δs = R ln 2 ≈ 199 J/kg K > 0. All of it is generated entropy, because no heat crossed the boundary.
- 1000 J flows from a reservoir at 500 K to one at 300 K: ΔS_hot = −2.0 J/K, ΔS_cold = +3.33 J/K, so ΔS_total = +1.33 J/K. The heat transfer is irreversible.

Isolated systems and maximum entropy
For an isolated system (no heat or work), ΔS ≥ 0. Treating a system plus its surroundings as an isolated "universe", every real process increases total entropy, and a process that would decrease it is impossible. An isolated system reaches equilibrium when its entropy is a maximum consistent with the constraints.

Molecular interpretation
Statistically, entropy measures the number of microscopic arrangements (microstates) consistent with the macroscopic state: Boltzmann's S = k ln Ω. Irreversible processes move systems towards overwhelmingly more probable macrostates. Free expansion increases entropy because the molecules have many more possible positions.

Using T–s diagrams
- The area under a reversible process on a T–s diagram is the heat transferred.
- For a reversible cycle, the enclosed area is the net work.
- Isentropic processes are vertical lines; a Carnot cycle is a rectangle.

Exam tips: entropy is a property, so to find Δs for an irreversible process, use any convenient reversible path between the same end states (or the perfect gas formulae). Then compare with ∫δQ/T to find the entropy generated.

notes.h: Reciprocating internal combustion engines: Otto and Diesel cycles
notes.body:
Reciprocating engines burn fuel inside a cylinder and use the expanding gases to drive a piston. Two types dominate:
- Spark ignition (SI, petrol/gasoline): a fuel–air mixture is compressed and ignited by a spark. Compression ratios are limited (typically around 8 to 12) by knock, the uncontrolled auto-ignition of the end gas.
- Compression ignition (CI, diesel): air alone is compressed to a high temperature, and fuel injected near the top of the stroke ignites spontaneously. Compression ratios are higher (typically about 14 to 22).

Terminology
- Bore, stroke, top dead centre (TDC), bottom dead centre (BDC).
- Swept volume V_s = V_BDC − V_TDC; clearance volume V_c = V_TDC.
- Compression ratio r = V_BDC/V_TDC = (V_s + V_c)/V_c.
- Four-stroke engines complete induction, compression, power and exhaust in two crankshaft revolutions.

Air-standard assumptions
To analyse the cycles simply, the working fluid is treated as a fixed mass of air, a perfect gas with constant specific heats. Combustion is replaced by heat addition from an external source, exhaust and induction by heat rejection at constant volume, and compression and expansion are reversible and adiabatic.

The Otto cycle (ideal SI engine)
- 1→2 isentropic compression; 2→3 heat addition at constant volume; 3→4 isentropic expansion; 4→1 heat rejection at constant volume.
- Since q_in = c_v(T₃ − T₂) and q_out = c_v(T₄ − T₁), and T₂/T₁ = T₃/T₄ = r^(γ−1):
- η_Otto = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1).
- Efficiency depends only on compression ratio (and γ). Example: r = 10, γ = 1.4 gives η = 1 − 10^−0.4 ≈ 0.602.

The Diesel cycle (ideal CI engine)
- As Otto, except heat is added at constant pressure (2→3), because fuel burns as it is injected while the piston moves down.
- Cut-off ratio r_c = V₃/V₂.
- η_Diesel = 1 − [1/r^(γ−1)] × (r_c^γ − 1)/[γ(r_c − 1)].
- The bracketed factor is greater than 1, so for the same compression ratio Diesel is less efficient than Otto. In practice diesel engines are more efficient because they run at much higher compression ratios.
- Example: r = 18, r_c = 2, γ = 1.4: η ≈ 1 − (1/3.178) × (2.639 − 1)/1.4 ≈ 0.632.

Mean effective pressure
The mean effective pressure is net work per cycle divided by swept volume: mep = W_net/V_s. It is a measure of how much work an engine of a given size produces and allows engines of different sizes to be compared.

Practical considerations
Real engines fall well below air-standard efficiencies because of:
- heat transfer to the cylinder walls;
- finite combustion time (heat is not added at exactly constant volume);
- pumping work during induction and exhaust, especially at part throttle in SI engines;
- friction, valve timing, and the variation of c_p and γ with temperature and composition.

Exam tips: draw the p–v and T–s diagrams first, label states 1 to 4, and use isentropic relations to step round the cycle. Make sure you can derive the Otto efficiency, not just quote it.

notes.h: Control volume analysis: the steady flow energy equation and entropy in flows
notes.body:
Most engineering devices (turbines, compressors, nozzles, heat exchangers, throttles) have fluid flowing through them, so we apply the laws of thermodynamics to a control volume.

Mass conservation revisited
In steady flow, Σṁ_in = Σṁ_out, with ṁ = ρAV.

The First Law for a control volume
Fluid crossing the boundary carries internal energy, kinetic energy and potential energy. It also does "flow work" pv per unit mass to push itself in or out. Grouping u + pv as enthalpy h, the steady flow energy equation (SFEE) for one inlet (1) and one outlet (2) is:
- Q̇ − Ẇ_x = ṁ[(h₂ + ½V₂² + gz₂) − (h₁ + ½V₁² + gz₁)]
- Q̇ is the rate of heat input and Ẇ_x the shaft work output (the work done by the fluid on moving blades, excluding flow work).
- For a perfect gas, Δh = c_pΔT. Stagnation enthalpy h₀ = h + ½V² is often used.

Standard applications
- Turbine (adiabatic, kinetic and potential energy changes small): Ẇ_x = ṁ(h₁ − h₂) > 0.
- Compressor or pump: work input = ṁ(h₂ − h₁).
- Nozzle (no work, adiabatic): V₂ = √[V₁² + 2(h₁ − h₂)]. The fluid accelerates as enthalpy falls.
- Throttle (valve or porous plug; no work, adiabatic, negligible velocity change): h₂ = h₁. For a perfect gas this means T₂ = T₁. Throttling is highly irreversible: pressure falls with no work recovered.
- Heat exchanger: no work; the enthalpy lost by one stream is gained by the other if the outside is insulated.

The Second Law for control volumes
Entropy flows in and out with the fluid. In steady flow:
- ṁ(s₂ − s₁) = ∫δQ̇/T + Ṡ_gen, with Ṡ_gen ≥ 0.
- For an adiabatic device, s₂ ≥ s₁: entropy can only increase through the device. If the flow is also reversible, it is isentropic.
- For a perfect gas: s₂ − s₁ = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁).

Isentropic efficiencies
Real adiabatic machines are compared with an ideal isentropic machine working between the same pressures.
- Turbine: η_T = actual work/isentropic work = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − h₂s).
- Compressor: η_C = isentropic work/actual work = (h₂s − h₁)/(h₂ − h₁).
- On an h–s diagram, the actual outlet state lies to the right of (at higher entropy than) the isentropic one.

Worked example
Air enters a compressor at 1 bar, 300 K and leaves at 10 bar. Isentropic outlet temperature: T₂s = 300 × 10^(0.4/1.4) ≈ 579 K. Isentropic work = c_p(T₂s − T₁) ≈ 1005 × 279 ≈ 281 kJ/kg. Note that this is larger than the closed-system adiabatic compression work (c_vΔT ≈ 200 kJ/kg), because the flow work of pushing the gas in and out is included in the enthalpy.

Steady reversible flow work
For a reversible steady flow with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, w_x = −∫v dp. This shows why pumping a liquid (small v) needs much less work than compressing a gas over the same pressure ratio.

Exam tips: always state what is neglected (heat loss, ΔKE, ΔPE) before simplifying the SFEE, and keep shaft work and flow work separate. Use h for flows and u for closed systems.

notes.h: The Joule (Brayton) cycle, gas turbines and jet engines
notes.body:
A gas turbine draws in air continuously, compresses it, burns fuel in it at roughly constant pressure, and expands the hot gas through a turbine that drives the compressor. In a power-generation gas turbine the surplus turbine work drives a generator; in a turbojet, the gas leaving the turbine is expanded through a nozzle to give a high-speed jet.

The ideal Joule (Brayton) cycle
Air-standard assumptions: air is a perfect gas with constant specific heats; combustion is replaced by heat addition at constant pressure; the exhaust and intake are joined by heat rejection at constant pressure.
- 1→2 isentropic compression (compressor)
- 2→3 heat addition at constant pressure (combustor)
- 3→4 isentropic expansion (turbine)
- 4→1 heat rejection at constant pressure
Using the SFEE for each component: w_C = c_p(T₂ − T₁), q_in = c_p(T₃ − T₂), w_T = c_p(T₃ − T₄).

Efficiency
With pressure ratio r_p = p₂/p₁, both isentropic processes have the same temperature ratio: T₂/T₁ = T₃/T₄ = r_p^((γ−1)/γ). Hence:
- η_Joule = 1 − T₁/T₂ = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ).
- Efficiency depends only on the pressure ratio; it rises as r_p rises.
- Example: r_p = 10, γ = 1.4: r_p^0.2857 ≈ 1.931, so η ≈ 0.482.

Specific work and the turbine entry temperature
Net work w_net = c_p[(T₃ − T₄) − (T₂ − T₁)]. With T₁ = 300 K, T₃ = 1400 K, r_p = 10: T₂ ≈ 579 K and T₄ ≈ 725 K, so w_net ≈ 1005 × (675 − 279) ≈ 398 kJ/kg. Heat input is 1005 × (1400 − 579) ≈ 825 kJ/kg, giving η ≈ 0.482 as expected.
- For fixed T₁ and T₃, the net work is a maximum when T₂ = √(T₁T₃) (equivalently T₂ = T₄).
- Higher turbine entry temperature T₃ gives more work per kg of air, so the engine can be smaller. It is limited by turbine blade materials and cooling.
- The back work ratio (w_C/w_T) is large, often 40 to 60% in practice, so component efficiencies matter a great deal.

Real cycles
With non-isentropic compression and expansion, T₂ is higher and T₄ higher than ideal. Net work falls and efficiency now depends on T₃ as well as r_p. Use T₂ = T₁ + (T₂s − T₁)/η_C and T₄ = T₃ − η_T(T₃ − T₄s).

The jet engine
In a turbojet the turbine produces just enough work to drive the compressor; the remaining enthalpy accelerates the exhaust in a nozzle.
- Thrust (ignoring fuel mass flow and pressure differences at the nozzle exit): F = ṁ(V_j − V₀), where V₀ is the flight speed and V_j the jet speed. This follows from the steady momentum equation.
- Background (a standard result, not named on the syllabus page): propulsive (Froude) efficiency η_p = 2V₀/(V₀ + V_j). It is high when the jet speed is only a little above the flight speed.
- So high thrust with high propulsive efficiency requires a large mass flow at modest jet speed. That is why modern airliners use high-bypass turbofans, where a large fan pushes a big mass of air at relatively low speed.

Exam tips: tabulate temperatures at states 1 to 4 and compute each component's work from the SFEE. Check that w_net = q_in − q_out. Remember that the Joule efficiency formula holds only for the ideal cycle.

questions.q: What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 10 m in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
questions.why: p_gauge = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98,100 Pa = 98.1 kPa. 9.81 kPa is the value at 1 m; 199 kPa is the absolute pressure (gauge plus about 101 kPa atmospheric), not the gauge pressure; 981 kPa is ten times too large.

questions.q: A vertical rectangular sluice gate 2 m wide holds back water 3 m deep on one side (air on the other). Where does the resultant hydrostatic force act?
options: 3 m below the surface (at the bed)
questions.why: The pressure distribution is triangular, so the resultant acts at its centroid, 2H/3 = 2 m below the surface. The centroid of the gate (1.5 m) is where the average pressure acts, but the centre of pressure is lower because pressure increases with depth.

questions.q: A block of wood (density 600 kg/m³) of volume 0.05 m³ floats in fresh water. (a) What fraction of its volume is submerged? (b) What extra downward force would just submerge it completely?
markScheme: States that a floating body displaces its own weight (Archimedes)
Fraction submerged = ρ_wood/ρ_water = 0.6
Full submersion buoyancy = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05 = 490.5 N
questions.modelAnswer: (a) In equilibrium the buoyancy equals the weight, so ρ_w g V_sub = ρ_b g V, giving V_sub/V = 600/1000 = 0.6. (b) Fully submerged, the buoyancy is 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05 = 490.5 N and the weight is 600 × 9.81 × 0.05 = 294.3 N, so an additional downward force of about 196 N is needed.

questions.q: A water jet of diameter 50 mm and speed 20 m/s strikes a large flat plate normally. What is the force on the plate, approximately?
questions.why: ṁ = ρAV = 1000 × π(0.025)² × 20 ≈ 39.3 kg/s and F = ṁV ≈ 785 N. 39 N is just the mass flow number; 393 N is half the answer; 1571 N is 2ṁV, which applies to a jet turned through 180°.

questions.q: In a steady-flow momentum analysis of a nozzle discharging to atmosphere, why can atmospheric pressure be ignored if gauge pressures are used throughout?
options: Because a uniform pressure acting over a closed surface gives zero net force
Because atmospheric pressure is small compared with the jet pressure
Because Bernoulli's equation already includes it
questions.why: A uniform pressure integrated over any closed surface gives zero net force, so it can be subtracted from all pressures. Incompressibility is irrelevant; atmospheric pressure is not necessarily small; Bernoulli is a separate equation and does not remove pressure forces from a momentum balance.

questions.q: Water flows steadily through a horizontal 90° bend. At inlet (flowing in +x) the diameter is 0.2 m, gauge pressure 150 kPa and speed 3 m/s; at outlet (flowing in +y) the diameter is also 0.2 m and gauge pressure 140 kPa. Find the x and y components of the force exerted by the fluid on the bend.
markScheme: Q = AV with A = π(0.1)² = 0.0314 m²; ṁ = 94.2 kg/s; outlet speed 3 m/s by continuity
x-momentum: p₁A₁ + F_x = ṁ(0 − V₁) gives F_x = −p₁A − ṁV = −4712 − 283 ≈ −4995 N on the fluid
y-momentum: −p₂A₂ + F_y = ṁV₂ gives F_y = p₂A + ṁV = 4398 + 283 ≈ 4681 N on the fluid
Force on the bend is equal and opposite: about +5.0 kN in x and −4.7 kN in y
Clear CV diagram and sign convention
questions.modelAnswer: A = π × 0.1² = 0.03142 m², ṁ = 1000 × 0.03142 × 3 = 94.25 kg/s, V₂ = 3 m/s. Let F be the force of the bend on the fluid. x: the inlet pressure force p₁A = 150,000 × 0.03142 = 4712 N acts in +x; outflow has no x-momentum, so 4712 + F_x = 94.25 × (0 − 3) = −283, giving F_x ≈ −4995 N. y: the outlet pressure force p₂A = 4398 N acts on the CV in −y; −4398 + F_y = 94.25 × 3 = 283, so F_y ≈ +4681 N. The force of the fluid on the bend is the reaction: about 5.0 kN in +x and 4.7 kN in −y (magnitude ≈ 6.8 kN).

questions.q: Which condition is NOT required for Bernoulli's equation p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant to hold between two points?
options: No work done on the fluid between the points (no pump or turbine)
The two points have the same velocity
questions.why: Bernoulli requires steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline with no shaft work or heat transfer. The points need not have the same velocity; the whole point is to relate differing speeds and pressures.

questions.q: Water flows in a 100 mm pipe through a venturi with a 50 mm throat. The pressure difference between pipe and throat is 15 kPa. Ignoring losses, what is the throat velocity?
questions.why: V₂ = √[2Δp/(ρ(1 − (A₂/A₁)²))] = √[30/(1 − 0.0625)] = √32 ≈ 5.66 m/s. 5.48 m/s (√30) ignores the upstream velocity; 2.83 m/s is half the correct value; 7.75 m/s (√60) double-counts the pressure term and does not come from combining Bernoulli with continuity.

questions.q: Water flows under a sluice gate in a wide horizontal rectangular channel. The upstream depth is 2.0 m and the downstream depth (at the vena contracta) is 0.4 m. Assuming no energy loss, find the flow rate per unit width and the downstream Froude number.
markScheme: Continuity per unit width: q = V₁h₁ = V₂h₂
Bernoulli on the free surface: h₁ + V₁²/2g = h₂ + V₂²/2g
V₂ = q/h₂ ≈ 5.72 m/s
Fr₂ = V₂/√(gh₂) ≈ 5.72/1.98 ≈ 2.89 (supercritical)
questions.modelAnswer: Continuity: V₁ = q/2, V₂ = q/0.4. Bernoulli along the free surface (pressure atmospheric): 2 + q²/(2g × 4) = 0.4 + q²/(2g × 0.16). So 1.6 = (q²/19.62)(6.25 − 0.25), giving q² = 5.23 and q ≈ 2.29 m²/s. Then V₁ ≈ 1.14 m/s and V₂ ≈ 5.72 m/s. Fr₂ = 5.72/√(9.81 × 0.4) = 5.72/1.98 ≈ 2.89, so the downstream flow is supercritical (upstream Fr₁ ≈ 0.26 is subcritical).

questions.q: Fluid flows round a bend with streamlines of radius R. How does the static pressure vary across the streamlines (ignoring gravity)?
options: It increases towards the centre of curvature
It increases away from the centre of curvature
It depends only on the fluid viscosity
It is uniform across the streamlines
questions.why: Normal to a streamline, ∂p/∂n = ρV²/R with n pointing away from the centre, so pressure rises outward; the inward pressure force supplies the centripetal acceleration. Uniform pressure applies only to straight streamlines; viscosity is not needed for this result.

questions.q: A tennis ball hit with heavy topspin dips more sharply than one without spin. Which effect explains this?
questions.why: Spin creates circulation and a sideways (here downward) force: the Magnus effect. The Coanda effect concerns jets following curved surfaces; the venturi effect is the pressure drop in a contraction; Archimedes' principle concerns buoyancy.

questions.q: Explain, with reference to the pressure field, why a jet of water from a tap will follow the curved back of a spoon held in it, and state what happens to the spoon.
markScheme: To follow the convex surface, the jet's streamlines must curve
Curved streamlines require a pressure gradient with pressure increasing away from the centre of curvature
The outer edge of the jet is at atmospheric pressure, so the pressure at the spoon surface must be below atmospheric
This low pressure holds the jet to the surface (the Coanda effect)
The net pressure difference across the spoon pulls it towards the jet
questions.modelAnswer: For the jet to bend round the convex back of the spoon, its streamlines must curve, which needs a pressure gradient ∂p/∂n = ρV²/R with pressure rising away from the centre of curvature. The free outer edge of the jet is at atmospheric pressure, so the pressure on the spoon's surface must be below atmospheric. This suction keeps the jet attached (the Coanda effect), and because atmospheric pressure acts on the other side of the spoon, the spoon is pulled into the jet.

questions.q: A perfect gas undergoes a reversible isothermal expansion in a closed system. Which statement is true?
questions.why: For a perfect gas u depends only on T, so ΔU = 0 at constant T and the First Law gives Q = W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁). Q = 0 describes an adiabatic process; W = 0 a constant-volume process; ΔH = Q holds for a constant-pressure process.

questions.q: Air (γ = 1.4) is compressed reversibly and adiabatically from 1 bar, 300 K to 10 bar. What is the final temperature, approximately?
questions.why: T₂ = T₁(p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ) = 300 × 10^0.2857 ≈ 300 × 1.931 ≈ 579 K. 3000 K assumes T ∝ p (as at constant volume); 754 K uses the exponent γ − 1 = 0.4, which goes with a volume ratio, not a pressure ratio; 300 K would be an isothermal compression, but an adiabatic compression must raise the temperature.

questions.q: 0.1 kg of air (R = 287 J/kg K, c_v = 718 J/kg K) at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed in a piston-cylinder polytropically with n = 1.3 to 8 bar. Find the work done on the air and the heat transfer.
markScheme: Work done by air W = mR(T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1) ≈ 0.1 × 287 × (−184.8)/0.3 ≈ −17.7 kJ, so about 17.7 kJ done on the air
Q = ΔU + W ≈ 13.3 − 17.7 ≈ −4.4 kJ: about 4.4 kJ of heat rejected
Correct sign convention stated
questions.modelAnswer: For a polytropic process T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)^((n−1)/n) = 8^0.2308 ≈ 1.616, so T₂ ≈ 484.8 K. Work done by the air W = mR(T₁ − T₂)/(n − 1) = 0.1 × 287 × (300 − 484.8)/0.3 ≈ −17.7 kJ, i.e. about 17.7 kJ of work is done on the air. ΔU = 0.1 × 718 × 184.8 ≈ 13.3 kJ. First Law: Q = ΔU + W ≈ 13.3 − 17.7 ≈ −4.4 kJ, so about 4.4 kJ of heat is rejected during the compression.

questions.q: An inventor claims an engine that takes 1000 kJ of heat from a source at 800 K, rejects heat to surroundings at 300 K, and produces 700 kJ of work. What is the verdict?
options: Impossible: it exceeds the Carnot efficiency of 62.5%
Possible only if the engine is reversible
Impossible: it violates the First Law
questions.why: η_Carnot = 1 − 300/800 = 0.625, so no engine between these reservoirs can exceed 62.5%. The claim (70%) violates the Second Law, not the First Law (energy balances if 300 kJ is rejected). Even a reversible engine can only reach 62.5%.

questions.q: What is the maximum possible COP of a heat pump delivering heat to a house at 20 °C while extracting heat from outside air at 0 °C?
questions.why: COP_HP,max = T_H/(T_H − T_C) = 293/20 ≈ 14.7 (kelvin must be used). 13.7 is the refrigerator COP T_C/(T_H − T_C) = 273/20. A COP of 1 corresponds to direct electric heating; an infinite COP would violate the Clausius statement.

questions.q: State the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements of the Second Law and show that a violation of the Clausius statement would allow a violation of the Kelvin–Planck statement.
markScheme: Kelvin–Planck: no cyclic device can produce net work exchanging heat with a single reservoir
Clausius: no cyclic device can move heat from cold to hot with no other effect
Suppose a device moves Q_C from cold to hot unaided
Couple it with an ordinary engine that takes Q_H from the hot reservoir, rejects Q_C to the cold one and produces W = Q_H − Q_C
The combination has no net exchange with the cold reservoir and converts Q_H − Q_C from the hot reservoir wholly into work, violating Kelvin–Planck
questions.modelAnswer: Kelvin–Planck: it is impossible for a device working in a cycle to produce net work while exchanging heat with only one reservoir. Clausius: it is impossible for a cyclic device to transfer heat from a colder to a hotter body with no other effect. Suppose a Clausius-violating device transfers Q_C from the cold reservoir to the hot one with no work. Run an ordinary engine alongside it that takes Q_H from the hot reservoir, produces W = Q_H − Q_C and rejects Q_C to the cold reservoir. The cold reservoir's net heat exchange is zero, so the combined device exchanges heat only with the hot reservoir (net Q_H − Q_C) and converts it entirely into work, which violates Kelvin–Planck. So the statements are equivalent.

questions.q: 1 kg of air expands freely (unresisted) into an evacuated insulated chamber, doubling its volume. Which is correct?
questions.why: No heat or work, so ΔU = 0 and for a perfect gas ΔT = 0. Entropy is a property: using a reversible isothermal path between the same states, Δs = R ln(v₂/v₁) = R ln 2 ≈ 199 J/kg K. 'Q = 0 so Δs = 0' applies only to reversible adiabatic processes; c_p ln 2 would be for doubling T at constant pressure.

questions.q: On a T–s diagram, what does the area under a reversible process curve represent?
questions.why: Since δq_rev = T ds, ∫T ds is the heat transferred in a reversible process. The enclosed area of a reversible cycle equals net work, but the area under a single process is heat. Entropy generated is zero for a reversible process.

questions.q: 1000 kJ of heat flows directly from a large reservoir at 600 K to a large reservoir at 300 K. Calculate the entropy change of each reservoir and of the universe, and comment.
markScheme: ΔS_universe = +1.667 kJ/K
Positive total shows the process is irreversible and allowed by the Second Law
Notes that a reverse flow from cold to hot would give a negative total and is impossible
questions.modelAnswer: Each reservoir is at uniform temperature, so ΔS = Q/T. Hot: −1000/600 = −1.667 kJ/K. Cold: +1000/300 = +3.333 kJ/K. Total: +1.667 kJ/K. The entropy of the universe increases, as it must for an irreversible process (heat transfer across a finite temperature difference). The reverse process would give −1.667 kJ/K and is forbidden by the Second Law (Clausius statement).

questions.q: What is the air-standard efficiency of an Otto cycle with compression ratio 10 (γ = 1.4)?
questions.why: η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1) = 1 − 10^−0.4 = 1 − 0.398 ≈ 0.602. 90% would be 1 − 1/r; 48% is the Joule cycle value for pressure ratio 10; 40% is 10^−0.4 itself.

questions.q: For the same compression ratio, how does the air-standard Diesel cycle efficiency compare with the Otto cycle?
options: It depends only on the bore and stroke
Diesel is higher, because heat is added at constant pressure
Diesel is lower, because the cut-off ratio factor exceeds 1
questions.why: η_Diesel = 1 − [1/r^(γ−1)] × (r_c^γ − 1)/[γ(r_c − 1)], and the factor (r_c^γ − 1)/[γ(r_c − 1)] > 1 for r_c > 1, so Diesel is less efficient at the same r. Practical diesels are more efficient because they use higher compression ratios.

questions.q: An air-standard Otto cycle has compression ratio 9. At the start of compression the air is at 1 bar and 300 K; the maximum temperature is 1800 K. Taking γ = 1.4 and c_v = 718 J/kg K, find T₂, T₄, the heat input, the net work per kg and the thermal efficiency.
markScheme: q_out = c_v(T₄ − T₁) ≈ 718 × 448 ≈ 322 kJ/kg, so w_net ≈ 452 kJ/kg
η = w_net/q_in ≈ 0.585, matching 1 − 9^−0.4

questions.q: A perfect gas passes through an insulated throttling valve with negligible change in velocity. What happens?
options: Temperature and entropy both stay constant
Enthalpy and temperature stay constant; entropy increases
questions.why: The SFEE with Q = W = 0 and negligible ΔKE gives h₂ = h₁; for a perfect gas h depends only on T, so T is constant. Pressure falls, so Δs = −R ln(p₂/p₁) > 0: throttling is irreversible. It is not isentropic.

questions.q: A turbine expands gas from 1200 K. The isentropic exit temperature would be 800 K and the actual exit temperature is 840 K. What is the isentropic efficiency (constant c_p)?
questions.why: η_T = (T₁ − T₂)/(T₁ − T₂s) = (1200 − 840)/(1200 − 800) = 360/400 = 0.90. 0.67 is just 800/1200, a ratio of absolute temperatures; 0.80 and 0.95 do not follow from the definition of isentropic efficiency.

questions.q: Air at 300 K and negligible velocity enters an adiabatic nozzle and leaves at 250 K. Taking c_p = 1005 J/kg K, find the exit velocity. If the nozzle were reversible, would the exit pressure be higher or lower than in an irreversible nozzle with the same exit temperature? Explain.
markScheme: SFEE with no work or heat: h₁ = h₂ + ½V₂²
Reversible adiabatic: s₂ = s₁; irreversible adiabatic: s₂ > s₁
From Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁), at fixed T₂ a larger Δs means a lower p₂

So the reversible nozzle reaches 250 K at a higher exit pressure (p₂/p₁ = (250/300)^3.5 ≈ 0.53) than the irreversible one; equivalently, friction means a bigger pressure drop is needed for the same exit speed
questions.modelAnswer: With Q̇ = Ẇ = 0 and V₁ ≈ 0, the SFEE gives ½V₂² = c_p(T₁ − T₂) = 1005 × 50 = 50,250 J/kg, so V₂ ≈ 317 m/s. This depends only on the temperature drop, so it is the same for a reversible or an irreversible nozzle reaching 250 K. For an adiabatic nozzle s₂ ≥ s₁, with equality only if reversible. Since s₂ − s₁ = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁), at fixed T₂ the entropy rise is larger when p₂ is smaller. The reversible (isentropic) nozzle reaches 250 K at p₂/p₁ = (250/300)^(γ/(γ−1)) = (0.833)^3.5 ≈ 0.53; an irreversible nozzle, with s₂ > s₁, reaches 250 K only at a lower exit pressure. So the reversible nozzle has the higher exit pressure. Put the other way, friction means a larger pressure drop is needed to produce the same exit velocity.

questions.q: What is the ideal Joule cycle efficiency for a pressure ratio of 10 (γ = 1.4)?
questions.why: η = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ) = 1 − 1/10^0.2857 = 1 − 1/1.931 ≈ 0.482. 60% is the Otto value for compression ratio 10 (exponent γ − 1 instead of (γ − 1)/γ). 90% and 37% have no basis.

questions.q: A jet engine moves 100 kg/s of air and produces a jet at 600 m/s while flying at 250 m/s. Using the simple momentum result, what is the thrust and the propulsive efficiency?
questions.why: F = ṁ(V_j − V₀) = 100 × 350 = 35 kN. η_p = 2V₀/(V₀ + V_j) = 500/850 ≈ 0.59. 60 kN ignores the flight speed; 85 kN adds the speeds; 42% is V₀/V_j.

questions.q: For an ideal Joule cycle with compressor inlet temperature T₁ and turbine inlet temperature T₃ fixed, show that the net specific work is a maximum when T₂ = √(T₁T₃).
markScheme: Let x = r_p^((γ−1)/γ), so T₂ = xT₁ and T₄ = T₃/x
w_net = c_p[(T₃ − T₃/x) − (xT₁ − T₁)]
dw_net/dx = c_p[T₃/x² − T₁] = 0
x² = T₃/T₁, so x = √(T₃/T₁)
Hence T₂ = xT₁ = √(T₁T₃) (and T₄ = T₂); second derivative negative so maximum
questions.modelAnswer: Let x = r_p^((γ−1)/γ). Isentropic relations give T₂ = xT₁ and T₄ = T₃/x. Net work w = c_p[(T₃ − T₄) − (T₂ − T₁)] = c_p[T₃ − T₃/x − xT₁ + T₁]. Differentiating: dw/dx = c_p[T₃/x² − T₁], which is zero when x² = T₃/T₁. The second derivative −2c_pT₃/x³ is negative, so this is a maximum. Then T₂ = xT₁ = √(T₁T₃), and T₄ = T₃/x = √(T₁T₃) too, so compressor and turbine exit temperatures are equal at maximum work.

questions.q:
Water flows steadily under a vertical sluice gate in a wide horizontal rectangular channel. Upstream of the gate the depth is 2.0 m; downstream, where the streamlines are again parallel, the depth is 0.4 m. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
(a) Explain why the pressure distribution is hydrostatic at the upstream and downstream sections, and why Bernoulli's equation may be applied along the free surface. [4]
(b) Find the flow rate per unit width and the velocities upstream and downstream. [6]
(c) Using a control volume, find the horizontal force per unit width exerted by the water on the gate. [7]
(d) Calculate the Froude numbers at the two sections and comment. [3]
markScheme: (a) Straight parallel streamlines: no pressure gradient across them other than hydrostatic, so p = ρg × depth below surface
(a) Free surface is a streamline at atmospheric pressure; flow steady, nearly inviscid accelerating flow, so h + V²/2g is constant along it
(b) q = V₁h₁ = V₂h₂ and h₁ + q²/2gh₁² = h₂ + q²/2gh₂²; q ≈ 2.29 m²/s
(c) Momentum per unit width: ½ρgh₁² − ½ρgh₂² − F = ρq(V₂ − V₁)
(c) ½ρgh₁² = 19.62 kN/m, ½ρgh₂² = 0.785 kN/m, ρq(V₂ − V₁) ≈ 10.46 kN/m
(c) F ≈ 8.37 kN per metre width, acting downstream on the gate; bed friction neglected
(d) Fr₁ ≈ 0.26 subcritical, Fr₂ ≈ 2.89 supercritical; the gate changes the flow from subcritical to supercritical at the same specific energy
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) At sections well upstream and downstream of the gate the streamlines are straight and parallel. With no streamline curvature there is no pressure gradient normal to the streamlines apart from that needed to support the fluid's weight, so pressure is hydrostatic: p = ρg × (depth below the surface). The free surface is itself a streamline on which the pressure is atmospheric. The flow from upstream to the vena contracta is a steady, accelerating flow with negligible friction, so Bernoulli applies along the surface streamline, giving h + V²/2g = constant.

(b) Continuity per unit width: q = V₁h₁ = V₂h₂. Bernoulli: h₁ + q²/(2gh₁²) = h₂ + q²/(2gh₂²). So h₁ − h₂ = (q²/2g)(1/h₂² − 1/h₁²): 1.6 = (q²/19.62)(6.25 − 0.25) = 0.3058q². Hence q² = 5.232 and q ≈ 2.287 m²/s. V₁ = 2.287/2.0 ≈ 1.14 m/s; V₂ = 2.287/0.4 ≈ 5.72 m/s. (Check: 2 + 1.144²/19.62 = 2.067 m; 0.4 + 5.718²/19.62 = 2.067 m.)

(c) Take a control volume from section 1 to section 2, bounded by the bed, the free surface and the gate. Horizontal forces on the water per unit width: the hydrostatic force at section 1, ½ρgh₁² = 0.5 × 1000 × 9.81 × 4 = 19,620 N, acting downstream; the hydrostatic force at section 2, ½ρgh₂² = 0.5 × 1000 × 9.81 × 0.16 = 784.8 N, acting upstream; and the force F from the gate on the water, acting upstream. Bed friction is neglected. Momentum: 19,620 − 784.8 − F = ρq(V₂ − V₁) = 1000 × 2.287 × (5.718 − 1.144) ≈ 10,461 N. So F ≈ 8,370 N per metre width. The water pushes the gate downstream with about 8.4 kN per metre width. This is less than a naive hydrostatic force on a gate holding back 2 m of still water, because the pressure on the gate's lower part falls as the flow accelerates.

(d) Fr₁ = V₁/√(gh₁) = 1.144/√(19.62) ≈ 0.26: subcritical. Fr₂ = 5.718/√(9.81 × 0.4) ≈ 2.89: supercritical. The gate converts slow, deep flow into fast, shallow flow at the same specific energy; the two depths are 'alternate depths' on either side of critical depth. Downstream, a hydraulic jump (with energy loss) would typically be needed to return to subcritical flow.

questions.q:
A simple gas turbine operates on a Joule cycle with air (c_p = 1005 J/kg K, R = 287 J/kg K, γ = 1.4). Air enters the compressor at 1 bar and 288 K; the pressure ratio is 12; the turbine inlet temperature is 1500 K. Pressure losses are negligible.
(a) Sketch the cycle on T–s axes, showing both the ideal and real compression and expansion processes. [4]
(b) For the ideal cycle, find the thermal efficiency. [3]
(c) The compressor and turbine have isentropic efficiencies of 0.85 and 0.90. Find the actual compressor and turbine exit temperatures, the net specific work and the thermal efficiency. [12]
(d) Calculate the entropy generated per kg of air in the compressor and comment on why the real efficiency is much lower than the ideal. [6]
markScheme: (a) T–s sketch: two constant-pressure lines; real compression and expansion lines slope to the right of the vertical isentropes
(c) w_C ≈ 352 kJ/kg, w_T ≈ 690 kJ/kg, w_net ≈ 338 kJ/kg
(c) q_in = c_p(T₃ − T₂) ≈ 866 kJ/kg; η ≈ 0.39
(d) Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁) ≈ 86.7 J/kg K; adiabatic so all generated
(d) Comment: large back work ratio (≈ 0.51) amplifies component losses; extra compressor work and lost turbine work reduce net output much more than heat input
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) On T–s axes draw two constant-pressure lines (1 bar and 12 bar), diverging as s increases. Ideal compression 1→2s is vertical; actual compression 1→2 ends at higher T and s on the 12 bar line. Heat addition 2→3 follows the high-pressure line to 1500 K. Ideal expansion 3→4s is vertical; actual expansion 3→4 ends at higher T and s on the 1 bar line.

(b) x = r_p^((γ−1)/γ) = 12^0.2857 ≈ 2.034. η_ideal = 1 − 1/x ≈ 1 − 0.4917 ≈ 0.508.

(c) Compressor: T₂s = 288 × 2.034 ≈ 585.8 K. T₂ = 288 + (585.8 − 288)/0.85 ≈ 288 + 350.3 ≈ 638.3 K. w_C = 1005 × 350.3 ≈ 352.1 kJ/kg.
Turbine: T₄s = 1500/2.034 ≈ 737.5 K. T₄ = 1500 − 0.90 × (1500 − 737.5) ≈ 1500 − 686.3 ≈ 813.7 K. w_T = 1005 × 686.3 ≈ 689.7 kJ/kg.
Net work: w_net ≈ 689.7 − 352.1 ≈ 337.6 kJ/kg.
Heat input: q_in = 1005 × (1500 − 638.3) ≈ 866.0 kJ/kg.
Efficiency: η ≈ 337.6/866.0 ≈ 0.39.

(d) The compressor is adiabatic, so the entropy generated equals the entropy rise of the air: Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁) = 1005 ln(638.3/288) − 287 ln 12 ≈ 1005 × 0.7958 − 287 × 2.4849 ≈ 799.8 − 713.2 ≈ 86.7 J/kg K. (The turbine similarly generates about 98.5 J/kg K.)
The efficiency falls from about 51% to 39% even though the components are 85 to 90% efficient. The reason is the large back work ratio: the compressor absorbs about 352/690 ≈ 51% of the turbine output. Compressor losses increase the work input, and turbine losses reduce the work output; both come straight off the net work, which is the small difference between two large numbers. The heat input falls only slightly (because T₂ is higher), so the efficiency drops sharply. Raising the turbine inlet temperature increases w_T relative to w_C and reduces this sensitivity, which is why turbine materials and cooling matter so much.
